items.body: Hundreds of Idahoans gathered in the rotunda of the Idaho Capitol on Jan. 12, 2026, to protest proposed cuts to the state's Medicaid program. The protest, organized by Idaho Voices for Children, took place before the governor's State of the State Address. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun) One thing we know for absolute certain in Idaho: Our people understand the value of Medicaid expansion. We voted to adopt Medicaid expansion in 2018 through ballot initiative started after years of inaction by the state Legislature, with more than 60 percent of Idaho voters supporting expanded healthcare access. When the state Legislature became very active in attempts to weaken and repeal that voter-approved expansion seemingly as soon as they could, Idahoans showed up. They traveled to Boise to let lawmakers know that the program was not a suggestion, but a mandate and more than 80,000 of our friends, family and neighbors relied on it. Idaho’s Medicaid work requirements start in January. Here’s how they will work. Some of the busiest days at the Capitol are when everyday Idahoans show up to have their voices heard on a healthcare bill when lawmakers have tried to repeal the program or institute confusing bureaucracy via work requirements. The halls are packed and hearing rooms overflow with Medicaid supporters who vastly outnumber those who advocate cuts at around 100-1 … and the one is very often not somebody from Idaho. Most Idahoans, myself included, don’t think much about the details of our health insurance until we need it. For someone with cancer, that could mean discovering at a doctor’s appointment, while scheduling a scan, or even in the middle of treatment or recovery that they no longer have Medicaid coverage due to the work requirements that will add red tape to the program starting in January. Then what? Do they delay treatment while trying to navigate the paperwork? Do they skip a follow-up appointment or prescription they can no longer afford? For most, there isn’t another insurance option waiting in the wings. These are Idahoans who already qualified for Medicaid, including people whose serious medical conditions should qualify them for a medical frailty exemption. Administrative red tape should not become another obstacle between a cancer patient and the care they need. When that happens, the consequences aren’t limited to the patient. Their families suffer too and local care providers must then care for somebody with no ability to pay the bill. It’s a terrible scenario and one Medicaid expansion has prevented from being widescale. This past session, House Bill 913 established the Jan. 1 start date for federally mandated work requirements. Medicaid proponents had requested a one-year extension to give the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and our residents more time to learn about the changes and implementation. That did not happen, so we hope Idaho lawmakers grasp fully their responsibility to hold true to the promises they made clearly and often during all those Boise debates over work requirements. Then, they were firm in their convictions that no eligible person would ever be stripped of healthcare. Policymakers should be just as committed now to making work requirement exemptions clear and accessible as they were about putting them into law. Coverage losses from work requirements usually aren’t because someone suddenly became ineligible, but because eligible people get caught in paperwork, reporting requirements, missed notices or other government bureaucracy. That distinction matters because it means people who are supposed to get care are forced to go without. Someone who otherwise could treat a medical condition and work, care for family members, and otherwise be active in their community could lose their coverage, get sicker until they can no longer work and be forced to a hospital and incur expensive medical debt, or worse. Officials with the League of Women Voters of Idaho said Little did not respond to their invitation to participate in the forum, though they left an empty chair open for him on the stage at South Junior High School in Boise in case he decided to participate. Pickens, a trial attorney and small business owner, said her first action if she is elected governor will be to present a state budget that restores the tax revenue and many of the budget cuts that Little and the Idaho Legislature cut during the 2026 legislative session. “It’s going to restore mental health funding,” Pickens said. “It’s going to restore Medicaid expansion. It’s going to restore full funding for public education, and that is critically important because the one thing I’ve heard across this state is Idaho families and the Idaho working class are hurting.” 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More Stegner, a retired Idaho Supreme Court justice, said his first action in office as governor would be to repeal the Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit, which Little signed into law as House Bill 93 in 2025. “I think my first executive action would be to try to bring litigation against the vouchers as best I could,” Stegener said. “I continue to believe that it’s unconstitutional that we are funding private school students and homeschool students when we’re not adequately funding our own public school students,” Stegner added. John Stegner is running for governor in 2026. (Photo courtesy of John Stegner) Little, Pickens, Stegner, Libertarian Paul Sand, a Constitution Party candidate who legally changed his name from Marvin Richardson to Pro-Life and independent write-in candidate named Jacob Burnett are all running for governor in the Nov. 3 general election. Tuesday’s candidate forum lasted 90 minutes and featured a question-and-answer format, with some questions submitted by audience members in attendance and others written by event organizers. “This is not a debate, it is a forum, an exchange of ideas, related to the issues confronting our beautiful state of Idaho,” League of Women Voters of Idaho President Jean Henscheid said at the beginning of Tuesday’s forum. Pickens, Stegner agree on many policy and budget issues Pickens and Stegner largely agreed on several of the issues, from supporting Proposition 1, the ballot initiative seeking to restore the right to an abortion in Idaho, to unanimously opposing both of the Idaho Legislature’s proposed constitutional amendments, House Joint Resolution 4 and House Joint Resolution 6. House Joint Resolution 4 would amend the Idaho Constitution so that only the Idaho Legislature could legalize marijuana, medical cannabis or other drugs. In doing so, House Joint Resolution 4 would also remove Idaho voters’ rights to run a ballot initiative to legalize marijuana, like voters in Oregon, Washington and several of Idaho’s neighboring states have done. House Joint Resolution 6 would amend the Idaho Constitution to make English the official language of Idaho. Pickens and Stegner said they will vote for Proposition 1 and implement it if it passes and will vote against HJR 4 and HJR 6. items.body: (UPDATED, 10:26 p.m. Tuesday, with Boise’s decision to cancel the homecoming football game.) Boise school officials have called off homecoming activities at Timberline High School, as police investigate an online threat targeting a Timberline student. According to an online petition, members of Timberline’s football team went on the Snapchat social media platform and “called for a female student to be raped and killed.” On Tuesday, Boise School District and Timberline officials said all homecoming events have been postponed, except for the homecoming dance, which was scheduled for Saturday. Originally, district officials had planned to postpone the homecoming football game, which had been scheduled for Thursday. But on Tuesday evening, the district canceled the game, which Timberline will now forfeit. “Given the seriousness of the circumstances involving recent student social media posts and ongoing concerns about student safety and well-being, we believe cancellation is the most responsible decision,” Superintendent Wendy Johnson, district Area Director Shelley Bonds and Timberline Principal Chad Wright said in an email to district families and staff. “Our priority is ensuring students and staff are safe and supported while providing the Timberline school community time to process what has occurred.” On Tuesday afternoon, in a separate email to Timberline families and staff, district and school leaders said “growing concerns over student safety” factored into their postponement decision. “This is not a decision made easily or lightly,” Johnson, Bonds and Wright wrote. “Homecoming is so much more than one game, one parade or one dance, it is a celebration of current, future and past students and the families, educators and community who support them. However, given the heightened emotions, threats of violence, and the simple need to pause, reflect and process, we believe it is not only the prudent decision, but the right one as well.” An “additional police presence” is on site at Timberline, district officials said in a question-and-answer page on the reported threat. Boise school officials have called the reported threat “disturbing.” However, the district and the Boise Police Department have said little about the case — which began to unfold Friday, when school officials contacted Boise Police’s school resource officer unit. “With an active investigation and the potential involvement of minors, we are limited to what we can share,” Johnson, Bonds and Wright said in a Sunday evening message to Timberline parents and staff. “While respecting privacy limits, we want to be as open, honest and transparent as possible to assure you that there is zero tolerance for the type of behavior and language attributed to any member of our school community. This is not who we are and we will not be defined by the actions of a few.” “Officers have been in contact with the Boise School District as part of the ongoing investigation,” Boise police said in a statement Monday. “We do not have additional details to share at this time.” Boise police had no new information on the investigation, spokeswoman Haley Williams said Tuesday afternoon. items.body: Last summer, Mackay High history teacher Jess Johnson listened to an audiobook about the USS Indianapolis on a trip home from Mount Rushmore. The story sparked Johnson’s interest in Lt. Cmdr. Earl Henry Sr., the ship’s dentist and an avid bird painter and taxidermist. Henry died after a Japanese submarine torpedoed the ship in July 1945. The ship sank in about 12 minutes, killing hundreds of crewmen. Johnson learned that Henry’s son, Earl Henry Jr., sold prints of his father’s work. One painting, “American Eagle in the Pacific,” was completed on the ship before it sank. It depicts an eagle holding a tattered Japanese flag. Johnson ordered a copy. “A nd maybe 20 minutes after I purchased it, he calls me,” Johnson said. The phone call kicked off a lifelong friendship between Johnson and Henry Jr. — and became the foundation for a unit in Johnson’s military history class at Mackay High. It’s just one of dozens of out-of-the-box approaches Johnson uses to bring history to life for his students. “It’s our lives — it’s what happens,” he said. “I try to make the connection between the old and the new.” Click to view slideshow. A teacher in the making Johnson grew up on a farm outside of Preston. He wasn’t “that good of a student” but sports had an impact. By eighth grade, his coaches influenced him to become a teacher. After high school, he started a family and worked nights as a cheesemaker. He fit classes into a busy schedule. With six kids, it took Johnson seven years to finish his teaching degree. He graduated from Utah State University in 1990 and took his first teaching job in Yuma, Arizona, the next fall. He taught middle school classes and coached at the high school. Coaching came easy — teaching did not. “I was drowning, and my principal said, ‘You’re not a very good teacher and you’re not going to make it,'” Johnson recalls. He eventually partnered with a veteran teacher, who encouraged him to be himself, stay calm, and push through ups and downs. That changed everything, Johnson said. He soon fell in love with the job — and with history. ‘I said heck yeah’ Johnson eventually made his way back to Idaho. After nearly two decades teaching at American Falls High, he and some other coaches earned their master’s degrees. He took a job as principal of Mackay High Jr./Sr. School, where his children graduated. Johnson moved around after becoming an empty nester. Three years ago, his sons moved back to Mackay and asked him to move closer. “I said heck yeah,” Johnson said. He returned to Mackay to teach history, government, and coach junior high school football — and continue his emphasis on projects. ‘I don’t go into the book’ “My style is probably different than a traditional history teacher,” Johnson said. “I don’t go into the book. I teach the standards and whatever, but my whole career has been hands-on projects.” Johnson has come up with dozens of projects over the years that tie into his history lessons. Students dress up as Roman soldiers with homemade armor, make hardtack, make their own gas masks to test with a fog machine, dress up as 1920s flappers and set up a faux speakeasy. At 65, the projects keep Johnson excited about teaching. “It really makes it meaningful,” he said. For him, history is key to helping students understand the world around them. Click to view slideshow. Henry Jr., now in his 80s, called in and shared stories about his father during Johnson’s unit on the USS Indianapolis. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idahoans voting in November’s general election will decide whether to give the Idaho Legislature the sole power to regulate marijuana and other drugs — and eliminate their right to bring a citizen-led ballot initiative to do so. 2026 Voter Guide Dat
items.body: A voter casts his ballot in the May 19, 2026, primary election at Emerson High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idahoans voting in November’s general election will decide whether to give the Idaho Legislature the sole power to regulate marijuana and other drugs — and eliminate their right to bring a citizen-led ballot initiative to do so. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More Currently, there are two ways in Idaho that marijuana, medical cannabis or other drugs can be legalized and regulated. First, the Idaho Legislature could pass a law to legalize it. Second, Idaho voters could legalize it by passing a ballot initiative. Who gets to decide is a big part of the debate over House Joint Resolution 4, or HJR 4 for short. House Joint Resolution 4 is a proposed amendment to the Idaho Constitution that would give the Idaho Legislature the sole authority and power to legalize marijuana (including medical marijuana), narcotics and other psychoactive substances. If a simple majority of voters vote “yes” for House Joint Resolution 4, Idahoans would not be allowed to bring a ballot initiative forward to legalize marijuana, medical cannabis, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. If voters vote “no” and don’t approve HJR 4, there would be no changes to the Idaho Constitution. That means Idahoans would still be able to use the ballot initiative process to legalize marijuana, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. Voters in several of Idaho’s neighboring states, including Washington, Oregon, Montana and Nevada, used ballot initiatives to legalize marijuana in those states. People have tried to do the same in Idaho. But so far, each effort has failed to meet the signature-gathering requirements to qualify for an election, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. SUBSCRIBE Passing HJR 4 would mean Idahoans voluntarily give up rights to ballot initiative process, Idaho constitutional scholar says David Adler, president of the nonprofit Alturas Institute in Idaho Falls, says passing HJR 4 would mean voters are agreeing to give up their own rights and freedoms. David Adler is president of the nonprofit Alturas Institute in Idaho Falls. (Photo courtesy of David Adler) Adler has taught courses on government and the Constitution at all three of Idaho’s public universities and has spoken about HJR 4 this fall. “The more I speak on it, the more I realize people generally are of the belief that this is about regulating marijuana and they don’t understand that it has a far broader impact on their ability to resort to the initiative to exercise their rights,” Adler said. “Really, HJR 4 asks Idahoans to surrender both their rights and their powers to shape their future,” Adler said. He said a ballot initiative is a tool of democracy that the public has used to improve the state since the 1930s. items.body: Joleen Noble, executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank, says the nonprofit organization typically provides more than 75,000 diapers to children in need per month. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Diaper Bank) As a mother of two small children (ages 2 and 5), there’s no need to lecture Jolleen Noble of Meridian about the cost of diapers – which could run close to $200 a month per child. And there’s no need to talk to her about other paycheck-eating costs such as daycare, medical emergencies and clothing. She knows all about the challenges of making ends meet. Noble, of course, can’t solve all of the financial problems. But as the executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank , she’s providing some welcome relief in at least one area. And there are no forms to fill out, or financial statements to submit. “People who need diapers need our help,” she said. There are limits. Noble’s nonprofit organization will provide up to 50 diapers a month per baby, which doesn’t cover the entire cost for diapers. But it does make the monthly diaper tab less daunting. “Diapers are expensive, and they just add to the cost of everything else,” she said. The diaper bank gets a large portion of its supply from the National Diaper Bank Network, buying bulk from manufacturers and regional diaper drives. Mary Kay Link, an Idaho Diaper Bank board member for seven years, sees how the organization helps mothers and families. She volunteers with the Holy Apostles St. Vincent de Paul of Meridian , one of 43 working partners that distribute diapers. “SVDP has many single moms who work and need food and diapers to make ends meet. Saving money on diapers allows them to use the money to pay bills or put gas in their car,” she said. Noble has been the executive director for almost a year, and demands for the service are growing. “When the diaper bank started in 2014, they were giving out 8,000 diapers a month, and when I started it was 50,000 per month. Typically, we give out 75,000 to 100,000 per month … last month we gave 119,000.” Noble says that level of growth would not happen without her board of directors. “We have an incredible all-volunteer board that has helped shape Idaho Diaper Bank into what it is today,” she said. “I would not be in the position I am today, or able to do what I do, without the support, leadership and willingness to jump in wherever they are needed.” The diaper bank’s 43 partners also contribute to the success. Susan Rohrbacher sees the needed help through Parma Community Schools, which serves more than 25 babies per month. “This partnership has been especially meaningful for families of children with special needs,” she said. “The Idaho Diaper Bank is truly making a difference by easing financial stress and helping our families feel supported and cared for.” As with other nonprofit organizations, Noble sees challenges. “The biggest need is sustainable funding that allows us to grow our reach. Our funding comes from grants and in-kind donations. There is no government assistance,” she said. “Simply put, if we want to send more diapers out the door, we have to bring more diapers and funding in the door,” Noble said. “Space is becoming another challenge. As we think about serving more families and potentially expanding, sustainable funding and the capacity to store the product becomes increasingly important.” One big way individuals and businesses can help is through diaper drives. “Some of my favorite moments are seeing people in the community rally around a diaper drive,” she said. “Those drives bring in product and monetary donations, of course, but they also get people talking about diaper needs and introduce people to our mission. items.body: Trained staff members could carry guns in the Marsing and Homedale school districts if local leaders move forward with safety programs modeled after one in the Kimberly district . As first reported by the Owyhee County Avalanche, Marsing Superintendent Norm Stewart and Homedale Superintendent Rob Sauer will present policies to their respective school boards this month that would lay out trainings for staffers selected to carry concealed firearms. Sauer will propose a policy for armed staff at a Monday, Oct. 12, board meeting. Stewart will propose a similar policy to Marsing trustees at a Tuesday, Oct. 13, meeting. Marsing’s plan would reflect Kimberly’s policy “ as much as possible,” Stewart said. That could mean adopting it entirely. Sauer said Homedale intends to do the same. The Kimberly district, located near Twin Falls, rolled out its program last year and modeled it after one at Xavier Charter School. In August, a gunman killed three people at an In-N-Out drive-thru in Twin Falls. At least three school shootings have occurred in Idaho throughout the last four decades, but none have resulted in a death. Most recently, in 2021 , a Rigby sixth grader shot two students and a custodian. All three victims survived non-life-threatening injuries. “ This is not something we’re excited about,” Sauer said. “ We just recognize the times we live in, and that we need to do our best to deter and delay so law enforcement can do their job and protect our students.” The policies would allow some staffers to carry concealed firearms on campus, Stewart and Sauer said. Staff members would first need an enhanced concealed carry permit from the county. County sheriffs issue the permits. In Owyhee County, where Marsing and Homedale are located, residents fill out a form to receive a permit. Staff members would then have to volunteer to carry a concealed weapon and receive approval from the school board. They would undergo a physical fitness exam, and the districts would hire a third party to perform psychological evaluations. Once volunteers pass their tests, they would begin 40 hours of training. Marsing and Homedale have not identified who would train the volunteers, but they anticipate working with the Owyhee County Sheriff’s Office. Volunteers would then have to complete at least 16 hours of additional training each year. The districts would pay for training and ammunition but would not buy guns or pay volunteers for their training hours. Volunteers would not receive extra pay. “This is strictly voluntary, and you’re doing it because you want to do it for the right reasons: protecting students and staff,” said Stewart. Neither superintendent had estimates for what the programs would cost. The programs are meant to supplement law enforcement, not replace it, district leaders explained. Armed staff members can buy time against an active shooter when police responses are slower in rural areas. Homedale has a police department of seven full-time officers, according to the agency’s website. Marsing has no police department, and the district’s school resource officer is an Owyhee County sheriff’s deputy, one of around 16 officers at the agency, according to 2024 budget reporting on Transparent Idaho . Gun ownership is prevalent in Idaho, where concealed carry is legal without a permit. A 2020 RAND Corporation study estimated around 0.6 guns per Idaho household. Guns are also a part of the state’s culture: In November, Idahoans will vote for the official state gun. School boards in some districts have allowed staff members to carry guns for more than a decade. In January, the West Ada district introduced armed security guards called “campus sentinels.” As state funding for schools stagnates and districts struggle to balance their budgets, school safety can take a hit. items.body: Idaho Speaker of the House Mike Moyle’s political action committee this month reported $43,440 in independent expenditures to support three Republican incumbents in swing districts. Moyle, R-Eagle, created Idaho Rising PAC in late 2023. During the 2024 election cycle, the PAC raised $467,286 and reported $431,984 in independent expenditures, including $321,000 in opposition to Proposition 1, the ranked-choice voting ballot initiative. This year, Moyle’s PAC isn’t raising or spending nearly as much on political ads. Here’s what this month’s filings show: $23,600 to support Rep. Mike Pohanka in District 26 Seat A Pohanka, seeking a second term, faces Democrat Anita Janis and independent Christian conservative Bella Schiffler. Click here to read more about the race. $11,340 to support Rep. Dustin Manwaring in District 29 Seat A Manwaring has served four terms in the House and faces a third matchup against Democrat Mary Shea, whom he defeated in 2024 by 10.4 percentage points. $8,500 to support Rep. Brandon Mitchell in District 6 Seat B Mitchell is running for a fourth term and will face Democrat Kathy Dawes in a rematch. He won in 2024 by 16.2 percentage points. Moyle’s PAC this year received contributions from Ketchum-based GR Squire LLC, developer Dan Richter, Idaho Realtors PAC, Marathon Petroleum Corp., Chevron, Big West Oil and Blue Cross of Idaho. Several other state legislators have PACs: Rep. Jordan Redman , R-Coeur d’Alene, spent $350,000 of his own money on the May primaries this year through his 36-18-1 Inc. PAC. Rep. Josh Tanner , R-Eagle, and Redman both lead the Idaho Summit PAC, which spent $217,757 on the primaries. Senate Pro Tempore Kelly Anthon , R-Declo, is chairman of Gem State Legacy Political Action Committee, which contributed $15,750 to candidates this year. Rep. Chris Mathis , D-Boise, registered Rising Tide Idaho PAC this year. He contributed $6,000 of his own money and has not reported any expenses.

Codi Galloway did not seek re-election this year in District 15, opening the seat for a race between Democrat Nancy Gregory, who just ended a 24-year run as a trustee for the Boise School District, and Republican Desi Burbank, the secretary of the Idaho PTA who previously served as a school board member on a North Carolina military base. items.body: The rotunda of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) When two mental health clinic owners in Idaho set out to restore critical services for people with severe mental illness, they faced an uphill battle. The Idaho Legislature was gearing up for across-the-board budget cuts. But Laura Scuri and Ric Boyce armed lawmakers with information and data — and spent time talking to journalists when four patients died after the mobile treatment service had been cut. Ric Boyce, director of Mental Health Specialists, testifies before the Idaho Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel on Dec. 15, 2025 in Rexburg. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The two often worked behind the scenes, directly with lawmakers instead of testifying before committees. “We formed individual relationships with half the Legislature pretty much,” Boyce recalled in an interview. In the end, the programs that they advocated served as a rare instance of a budget cut that state lawmakers reversed. On the final day of this year’s legislative session, Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed into law a bill that temporarily restored funding for the programs that the two providers pushed for: the Assertive Community Treatment program, a mobile program for people with severe mental illness, and peer support services, which helps people navigate treatment. After four patients died, Idaho governor approves restoring cut Medicaid mental health programs Now, a mental health nonprofit plans to honor the two. This week, the National Alliance on Mental Illness of Idaho plans to award them both the Kathie Garrett Impact Award, named after a former Idaho lawmaker. In a news release, the nonprofit said the duo’s advocacy “led to the return of those programs.” The award came as a surprise. “I don’t think either one of us were thinking for a second it’s something that would be noticed,” said Boyce, a clinical social worker who owns Mental Health Specialists, a clinic in eastern Idaho’s Chubbuck. “What was important to us was that we were able to get the clients we were working with back into the program they needed so badly. And that was enough.” Scuri, who co-owns Access Behavioral Health Services in Boise, said it’s her first award. “So it’s extra special to me — especially with the environment that we’re in, and all the changes,” she said. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Boyce said providers often feel like government decisions are final. But he said this experience tested that conception. “What I learned was that there are ways to make change happen even when it seems hopeless,” he said. But to do that, he said, requires a lot of work — and help. While he and Scuri were talking with lawmakers, he said they also found lawmakers coming to them for answers — to questions raised by community members in letters and direct outreach on all sorts of Medicaid changes, not just the cuts they were focused on. “Even individual advocacy, of sending a single letter, cumulatively had an effect. And those things were changing the minds of legislators,” Boyce said. Laura Scuri, co-owner of Access Behavioral Health Services, testifies before the Idaho Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel in Rexburg on Dec. 15, 2025. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Their advocacy experience taught Scuri to approach change as a process. “And really understanding that, as you go through that process, it’s not always gonna feel like you’re gonna get that change,” she said. “And so really staying in it, even though it gets really hard, and there are times when you don’t think you can overcome all the barriers.” And she said education is a big part of advocacy. items.body: A nine-member committee will begin the search for a new University of Idaho president . The State Board of Education announced the committee Friday, marking the first significant public step in the search. Current U of I President C. Scott Green announced his retirement on Sept. 9 ; he will stay on as president at his alma mater until June 30. Two State Board members will head the search: Shawn Keough of Sandpoint will chair the committee, and Pete Koehler of Caldwell will serve as vice chair. Koehler is a U of I alum. Here’s a look at the rest of the committee members: Chandra Zenner Ford, the U of I’s senior associate to the president, and executive officer of the university’s Boise and Southwest Idaho center. Mya Pronschinske Groza, a U of I marketing professor, and associate dean of the College of Business and Economics. Bill Gilbert, a former State Board member and a 1997 U of I graduate. Phil Reberger, who served as chief of staff to former Idaho Gov. and Sen. Dirk Kempthorne and former Idaho Sen. Steve Symms. Reberger is a 1964 U of I graduate. Clint Marshall, chair of the University of Idaho Foundation. Mary Hasenoehrl, owner of GKH Farms and partner in Gross Farms, Wilder. Dave Whitehead, president of Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories, Pullman, Wash. “We are grateful to these Vandals and community leaders for agreeing to serve,” State Board President Kurt Liebich said in a news release. “President Green has put the university in a strong position, and we are committed to a thorough search that finds a leader who can build on that momentum.” The timetable for the search is not set. However, the U of I has said the State Board hopes to fill the post by spring, before Green’s retirement. Under a new state law , passed this year, the presidential search process is now almost entirely a closed-door process. After private meetings and interviews, the search committee will submit a sole finalist’s name to the State Board. If board members agree to the recommendation, the board can publicly name the finalist and make the hire within 10 business days. The law also sets the guidelines for the makeup of a search committee, composed of at least eight members. With nine members, the U of I committee is slightly larger than the minimum required by law.

items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Two days after a grand jury indicted a former Idaho state government employee on two felony counts of misuse of public funds, a local judge dismissed the case — after a request from the prosecutor. The case marked the first criminal charges — and a rare public update — to emerge from a yearslong investigation launched by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador that probed how the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare doled out $72 million in federal child care grants in 2021 and 2022. The official who was criminally charged, Ericka Rupp, oversaw the grant program. In the indictment, filed in Canyon County District Court last week, the grand jury charged Rupp with two felony counts of misuse of public funds and securities, for allegedly illegally authorizing, appropriating or otherwise misusing more than $300 of the government’s money. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador speaks at the Idaho Medal of Honor ceremony held Sept. 1, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office) Labrador’s special prosecutor, Canyon County Prosecuting Attorney Christopher Boyd, told the Idaho Capital Sun that the amount of money allegedly misused was not specified in the indictment, but that it would’ve been an issue to determine during a potential trial. Boyd said he moved to drop the indictment based on feedback from jurors. “I, however, asked of them whether they felt the case was one worth pursuing in terms of resources,” Boyd wrote in a text message. “I truly wanted their opinion on this. They had spent several full days taking testimony. The majority of jurors felt my time was better spent focusing on the many other serious crimes they worked on.” For each count, the penalties could have been up to 14 years imprisonment and up to $10,000 in fines, according to state laws cited in the indictment. Rupp’s attorney, Scott McKay, declined to comment. In a Friday order, Third District Judge Thomas W. Whitney wrote he was dismissing the case upon the state’s request. The court hasn’t released records supporting the judge’s decision to dismiss the case. Special prosecutor Christopher Boyd argues in district court that the Idaho Office of the Attorney General should not pay legal fees associated with litigation that set to block the office’s civil subpoena. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Pending permission from the court, Boyd said he hopes to release a report with more details in the coming days. Asked whether he’d pursue charges against Rupp, or other people linked to the investigation, Boyd said: “The report should conclude my investigation.” The Idaho attorney general’s office could not immediately be reached for comment. Department of Health and Welfare spokesperson Greg Stahl directed questions about the case to parties involved. “(The Department of Health and Welfare) takes seriously its responsibility to be a good steward of taxpayer dollars and remains committed to transparency, accountability, and the appropriate use of public funds,” Stahl said in a statement. Hickman is an Idaho attorney with two decades of experience, including at global tech company Micron, and has served as board chair of Mormon Women for Ethical Government. Labrador is a former Idaho congressman and an immigration attorney. He became the state’s attorney general in 2023, after defeating the state’s longest-serving attorney general, Lawrence Wasden, in the Republican primary election. Wasden was among the pack endorsing Hickman. At the press conference, he and former Idaho Republican Attorney General Jim Jones, who also served as a state Supreme Court justice, cheered by her side. items.body: Few things are bipartisan anymore, but on Monday, the U.S. Senate overwhelmingly agreed on a college athletics makeover. Jeramiah Dickey More money for student-athletes. Less money for agents. Fewer player transfers. Limits on conference realignment. Protections for the non-revenue Olympic sports that now exist — precariously — under the inescapable shadow of football. Would it all affect college sports in Idaho? Absolutely. And should you care about all of that, even if you don’t care about college sports? Also, absolutely. An athletic program isn’t an entity unto itself. Increasingly, colleges and universities are looking to athletics as a revenue generator. This isn’t new: athletic success has long equated to increases in applications, enrollment and donor support. Now, colleges and universities want to use their athletic facilities to rake in revenue, and not just on game day. They want their facilities to bring in concerts and corporate retreats and support lucrative on-campus development. That long game hinges on staying competitive on turf and hardwood. Which puts college athletics in the unnatural position of hoping Congress will come to the rescue. “We’re living insanity, and the fact that the federal government’s having to get involved at all, I think, tells that story,” Boise State University athletic director Jeramiah Dickey told EdNews Thursday. What happened in Congress, and what happens next Monday’s 77-22 Senate vote was noteworthy — especially considering how much the sponsors crammed into the Protect College Sports Act . Far from a do-nothing bill, it tries to solve all of college sports’ problems in one shot. One big change: The bill will allow a college to pay its student-athletes up to $49 million a year, shattering the current $21 million “revenue sharing” cap. That higher cap would apply to everyone — but practically speaking, it may only be an issue in the NCAA’s so-called “Power Four” conferences, the Big Ten, the Southeastern Conference, the Big XII and the Atlantic Coast Conference. Terry Gawlik University of Idaho athletic director Terry Gawlik doesn’t expect to see her Big Sky Conference brethren bumping up against a $49 million cap. “They can make the cap as high as they want it for the Power Four, but we’re never going to get to that level of paying student athletes,” she said this week. “So that’s not something that affects us daily.” But the $49 million cap could affect Boise State. The Broncos made the first 12-team College Football Playoff two years ago and are contenders again this year — and landing in the CFP will pit Boise State against big-money programs that could push up to the salary cap. (Boise State paid its student-athletes $10 million last budget year.) Dickey said he’s “not a huge fan” of the $49 million cap, but he’s glad to see the bill set some kind of maximum. Both Gawlik and Dickey like another key piece of the bill. It would allow student-athletes to transfer once in their college careers — and force repeat transfers to sit out a season. The limits on transfers will restore stability in the locker room, Gawlik said. In a related vein, Dickey likes the limited, five-year window for athletes to complete their playing careers. “This is a chapter,” he said. “This is not forever.” The bill also sidesteps a political minefield: state laws restricting transgender athletes. As Politico reported last month , co-sponsor Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, inserted language clarifying that the federal law would not supersede state bans on transgender athletes. For Gov. Brad Little, who signed the nation’s first transgender athletics ban into law in 2020 , that’s a non-negotiable, spokeswoman Emily Callihan said this week. “Gov. Little remains strongly committed to defending women’s sports,” she said. What happens next to this bill, and all its pieces, is anyone’s guess. items.body: The Idaho Education Association (IEA) is cutting about 13% of its staff and closing its regional offices, leaders of the statewide teachers’ union announced this week. The cost-cutting measures come after union members told IEA’s board of directors to take a closer look at the organization’s budget and after a new law restricting taxpayer support for teachers’ union activities took effect. IEA is eliminating four union organizer positions, according to Executive Director Paul Stark. It’s also closing five regional offices, “centralizing operations in its Boise office.” And it’s turning Summer Institute, an annual professional development event, into an every-other-year event. IEA’s board of directors announced the cuts in an email to union members Monday. The board includes two dozen people, most of whom represent nine different geographic regions of the state. “Over the summer, we, your elected Board of Directors, carefully considered several options, asked difficult questions, and made decisions to put IEA on stronger financial footing for the future,” the board’s email said. “These decisions were not made lightly. They affect people. People who have dedicated themselves to serving our members and our profession.” Paul Stark, executive director of the Idaho Education Association " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-701x1180.jpg" class="wp-image-44392 size-thumbnail" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-119x200.jpg" alt="" width="119" height="200" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-119x200.jpg 119w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-368x620.jpg 368w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-701x1180.jpg 701w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-913x1536.jpg 913w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-1217x2048.jpg 1217w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/Paul-Stark-scaled.jpg 1521w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 119px) 100vw, 119px" /> Paul Stark, executive director of the Idaho Education Association The cuts followed a directive from IEA’s Delegate Assembly, a gathering of hundreds of local union leaders, the email said. In April the assembly told the board to “thoroughly examine” IEA’s budget and ensure that the union was “operating within its means.” The board also considered “the challenges created by recent legislative policies, including House Bill 516 ,” the email said. Enacted during this year’s legislative session , House Bill 516 prohibited public schools from using taxpayer-funded resources, such as payroll systems, to accommodate union activities. The Delegate Assembly issued a vote of no confidence in Gov. Brad Little for signing the “union-busting” bill into law. It took effect July 1. It’s unclear to what extent HB 516 factored into the downsizing. Among other restrictions, the law prohibits school districts from using payroll systems to deduct union dues. Districts also can’t offer teachers paid time off to engage in union activities unless IEA reimburses the district. And districts can’t give the union teachers’ contact information without their consent. The Freedom Foundation — an anti-union think tank based in Olympia, Wash. — for years lobbied lawmakers to enact the restrictions after it published a report arguing that Idaho unions were benefiting from government funds, facilities, resources and personnel. IEA leaders have repeatedly said that the union doesn’t receive taxpayer funding. But Stark didn’t provide specifics on how the law factored into the layoffs and office closures. “Idaho students and educators are only one month into the new school year, so the full effects of HB 516 on public education and the IEA have yet to be seen,” he said in an emailed statement Wednesday.

items.body: A televised state superintendent’s debate is off, after incumbent Debbie Critchfield backed out this week. Critchfield, a Republican, had originally agreed to an Oct. 12 debate against Democratic nominee Becky Sundin Mitchell, sponsored by KTVB. Critchfield now says she will not appear unless a third-party candidate — Constitution Party nominee Teresa Roundy — is also on the stage. The news comes barely a week after Critchfield and Sundin Mitchell appeared at a debate co-sponsored by Idaho EdNews and The College of Idaho . Roundy did not qualify for the Sept. 22 debate, since her campaign did not meet the co-sponsors’ fundraising threshold. The KTVB debate had a similar fundraising threshold, one the station says it has had in place for decades . Roundy’s campaign has not raised or spent any money, according to Idaho sunshine reports. In a statement to KTVB, Critchfield said her decision “isn’t about avoiding a debate,” but is instead about respecting the voters and the process. “There are three candidates in this race, and I believe voters deserve the opportunity to hear from all three,” Critchfield said in a statement to KTVB. “It’s not my place — or anyone else’s — to decide for voters which candidates are viable enough to be heard.” In a statement, Sundin Mitchell said Critchfield should be willing to answer questions about her record. “KTVB set its criteria for participation, and her decision to withdraw means Idaho voters will no longer get the opportunity to hear the candidates answer questions side by side,” Sundin Mitchell said. “Debates matter because elected officials should be willing to defend their records directly to the people they serve.” With the KTVB debate cancelled, Critchfield and Sundin Mitchell will probably not square off again before the Nov. 3 general election. The candidates have no other debates scheduled in the remaining five weeks of the campaign. The cancellation continues what has become an election-year trend. Debates between statewide candidates, once commonplace, have been nearly nonexistent this fall. Several Republican incumbents have refused to debate their opponents — rejecting or ignoring invitations to joint events. Gov. Brad Little, U.S. Sen. Jim Risch and Attorney General Raúl Labrador are unlikely to debate their opponents before the election. Consequently, the League of Women Voters has instead sponsored open forums, not debates, for whichever candidates decide to attend. An Oct. 6 Boise forum will feature Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens and independent candidate John Stegner; Little has not responded to the invitation. items.body: State Rep. Steve Berch, D-Boise, asks a question during the March 16, 2026, Idaho House Local Government Committee meeting at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) An incumbent Boise state representative who lives in a competitive legislative district has raised the most money of any candidate for the Idaho Legislature in 2026, online state campaign finance records show. Rep. Steve Berch, D-Boise, has raised $212,580.79 as of Tuesday afternoon. Although Republicans control a supermajority in the Idaho Legislature, Berch is the only candidate in Idaho’s 105 legislative districts who has raised more than $200,000 this year. Search Idaho campaign finance records online To search through finance records for each Idaho candidate, go to Idaho Sunshine, the Idaho Secretary of State’s campaign finance website . Through Idaho Sunshine, the public can search for candidates, political action committees, campaign expenditures, campaign contributions, reports and more. Berch also raised the most money heading into this year’s primary elections , the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. In an interview Tuesday, Berch attributed his fundraising success to engaging directly with voters and knocking on tens of thousands of doors in his legislative district. “It’s really very humbling, and it tells me that people like what I’m doing in terms of knocking on doors, holding in-person town hall meetings and sending out very detailed newsletters so they know the reason why I vote the way I do,” Berch said. Most of Berch’s campaign contributions came from people and from within Idaho. According to online state campaign finance reports, Berch raised $153,816 from people, $27,450 from companies, $9,000 from political committees and $1,000 from Democratic central committees. Berch raised $169,226 in Idaho and $22,040 from out-of-state donors, records show. The rest of Berch’s campaign money was un-itemized. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More Berch represents District 15 in west Boise, which has flipped back and forth between Democratic and Republican control since at least 2018. Berch’s opponent in the Nov. 3 general election, Republican Steve Keyser, has reported raising $13,592.67. District 15 is one of the rare truly split legislative districts in Idaho. For the past two years, Berch held one of the legislative seats in District 15 while Republicans held the other two. Two years before, Berch and the Democrats controlled two of the district’s seats while Republicans held just one. For that reason, both Republicans and Democrats will be looking to pick up a seat in District 15 in November’s general election What other Idaho legislative candidates are raising the most money Among the 10 Idaho legislative candidates who raised the most campaign money in 2026, seven are Republicans and three are Democrats. In total, six candidates have reported raising more than $100,000 in campaign money this year. Although it was decided months ago, Idaho’s primary election appears to have played a big role in campaign fundraising this year. Two candidates from the Republican primary election for Idaho Senate District 1, Sen. Jim Woodward and former Sen. Scott Herndon, were among the top four legislative candidates in terms of campaign fundraising for 2026. Herndon won the primary in May and advanced to the Nov. 3 general election, where he is running against independent candidate Steve Johnson. Legislative leadership positions also may have played a role in campaign fundraising this year. Some of the Idaho Legislature’s top ranking members, including House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star; Senate President Pro Tem Kelly Anthon, R-Rupert; and Senate Minority Leader Melissa Wintrow, D-Boise, all made the top 10 list for fundraising for legislative candidates this year. The League of Women Voters and Caldwell chamber hosted a U.S. Senate candidate forum Sept. 30 at Caldwell City Hall. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Three out of four candidates running to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate discussed their differing approaches on tariffs, military actions, immigration, and more Wednesday night in Caldwell. The race’s incumbent, Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, declined to participate. Independents Todd Achilles and Natalie Fleming, and Libertarian Matt Loesby, spoke at the forum hosted by the League of Women Voters, Caldwell Chamber of Commerce and the local American Association of University Women at Caldwell City Hall. 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More The three candidates differed in their proposals to address the federal budget deficit, reform immigration, and rein in military action abroad. Risch’s campaign manager Marc Kilmer told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email that Risch didn’t participate because, “It was organized by someone who has publicly endorsed our opponent, and therefore we felt it would not be an impartial debate.” Kilmer said the endorsement came from former Idaho Republican state Rep. Julie Yamamoto of Caldwell, but it wasn’t clear how she was connected to the organizers. He couldn’t immediately be reached to clarify. League of Women Voters of Idaho President Jean Henscheid told the Sun she didn’t know of any organizers that endorsed a candidate in the race. To watch the entire forum, visit the City of Caldwell Youtube page . How would the candidates address the high cost of living and tariffs? All of the candidates agreed that the existing 50% tariff on a range of Canadian good s, should be rolled back and implemented more strategically. Achilles argued that Congress needed to “take back control” of tariff policy from the White House, and manage them in a “more strategic way” to protect domestic industries. “Congress needs to stand up and be an independent branch of government, and execute their constitutional duties, which is to be in control of tariffs,” he said. Loesby argued that tariffs were a small part of the problem when it came to addressing high costs of living for Americans. He agreed that the existing high tariffs should be rolled back and the taxes on imported products should be used to address trade imbalances with China. To address cost of living challenges, he said the U.S. needed to “end all these horrific foreign wars,” and “deport the millions of people who should not be in our country” to address housing costs. Fleming called the trade war with Canada, who imposed retaliatory tariffs against the U.S., “mind-boggling,” and said the import taxes should be rolled back. items.body: Blue Cross of Idaho has denied some medical claims for employees and dependents in Coeur d’Alene after school district leaders refused to sign a contract to make monthly payments to cover their portion of the Idaho School Benefit Trust’s $13 million shortfall. But the district is still not signing the 12-month binding contract addendum, according to a letter Superintendent Shon Hocker sent to all district employees on Wednesday. The letter states the district learned that some employees have received claim denials or notices from Blue Cross, or their providers, for July and August claims. “We understand and share the concern and frustration this may cause,” Hocker wrote to his employees. Trustees conducted an emergency meeting Tuesday, which was not livestreamed or recorded, and voted to authorize the district to negotiate a “modified agreement that allows us to make monthly payments without compromising our legal standing.” “If a fair resolution cannot be reached quickly, the Board authorized the district to pay the full lump sum to ensure our employees’ claims are processed without delay,” Hocker wrote. items.body: With help from the Legislature, Idaho’s largest school district has the lowest property tax rate in the state and can build two new buildings over the next year without increasing its local tax burden. At a time when bonds and levies are hard to pass, West Ada School District trustees on Monday night approved a complicated loan agreement that will give the district $56.4 million in cash. The money will help the district turn a vacant warehouse into a career and technical education center on Locust Grove and rebuild Lake Hazel Elementary, with both projects expected to open in fall 2027. The district will pay the loan off over 15 years with ongoing state facilities funding. West Ada CFO Dave Roberts said the district expects at least $35.8 million in sales tax every year from House Bill 292 , passed in 2023. The bill was designed to reduce school districts’ property tax burden. A fraction of that annual appropriation, $5.3 million, will pay off the loan without increasing property taxes. “It’s possible that with this type of funding that West Ada may be able to build buildings without ever going to taxpayers again,” Roberts told EdNews on Tuesday. The projects follow the district’s recent completion of Independence Elementary in Star, which was built with state modernization funds from House Bill 521 and without an increase in property taxes. West Ada trustee David Binetti used props to show the relative difference in tax rates and test scores between West Ada and Boise school districts. He said he used Claude AI to gather the data. In a student survey last fall, 46% of Notus junior high school and high school students listed mental health as a concern. District Superintendent Jen Wright thought she had found a partial solution. She wanted to use $60,000 in federal grants to hire a behavioral health coordinator for preschool through 12 th grade. But last week, legislators tabled the program, leaving Notus and nine other rural schools shut out on funding. “I was really thinking that we were going to get it,” Wright said in an interview Tuesday. “It’s just very disappointing.” Until last week, the Department of Health and Welfare was pursuing a $1.2 million behavioral health hub program — designed to offer optional in-person or telehealth services to students and families. The money was going to come from a fraction of Idaho’s $186 million federal rural healthcare transformation grant . The Legislature’s Rural Health Transformation Committee abruptly put the behavioral health hub proposal on hold Friday — shifting the $1.2 million out of the program. Committee members noted that the Legislature had rejected a similar proposal in 2024 . Before Friday’s vote, nine districts had applied for behavioral health grants: Aberdeen, American Falls, Cascade, Castleford, Garden Valley, Marsing, Notus, Snake River and Wilder. Heritage Academy Public Charter in Jerome also applied. All the applicants were rural — and some distance from the closest clinic. In Notus’ case, the nearest mental health services are in Caldwell, a half hour drive away. Aberdeen School District Superintendent Scott Muir was hoping to use a $110,000 grant to bridge the gap between his rural community and health services in American Falls, about 20 minutes away, and Pocatello, about 50 minutes away. The grant would have gone toward new mental health and wellness services, additional counseling support and facilities upgrades. “We believe these efforts would have had a meaningful impact on the overall well-being of our students and community,” Muir said in an email to EdNews Tuesday. Friday’s committee vote came as a surprise to Wright. She said she only learned Notus had lost out on its grant through EdNews’ coverage of the hearing. The sudden news means Notus will look for other options. A new partnership with Insight Counseling — a third party that already works with Marsing and Wilder — will provide Notus with a clinical counselor. Without a $100,000 federal grant, American Falls will look at other ways to serve students and families in need, Superintendent Randy Jensen said Wednesday. “I also hope the state continues looking at more upstream approaches to student mental health and behavioral needs,” Jensen said. “If we can provide stronger support to children and families when students are younger, we may be able to prevent some of the more significant challenges that require intervention later. Prevention should be an important part of this conversation.” The Marsing School District applied for an $89,028 grant, and on Wednesday afternoon, Superintendent Norm Stewart called the committee’s decision ironic. “During the last legislative session, we were told that a state-mandated 60 seconds of silence would help positively impact student mental health. items.body: Idaho showed a 66% rise of 18 and 19-year-old registered voters between 2018 and 2022. Then, in 2023, Idaho legislators passed new voting laws targeted at student voters. After the laws took effect, Idaho saw a 23% decline in 18- and 19-year-old registered voters. Idaho is now last in the nation in the percentage of 18-year-old registered voters compared to registered voters aged 45 and older. Despite zero evidence of Idaho students fraudulently using their student IDs to vote, the law removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification. Previously, students could use their ID as a form of identification for registering to vote, and to vote on election day. BABE VOTE and the League of Women Voters of Idaho challenged the laws in court. However, our case was dismissed without a trial. If granted a trial, we would have shown evidence of legally eligible Idaho voters who were unable to vote under the new laws. Upon pushback from the community, Representative Brent Crane (R-Nampa) who helped pass the laws, said,“[the laws] were doing exactly what they were designed to do.” We continue to hear positive messages from our Secretary of State about how easy it is for Idahoans to register and vote. But for some legally eligible Idahoans, it has not been easy. Although these laws specifically targeted students, they have created barriers for other Idahoans—including people who have moved, changed their names, or no longer drive. Sam Sandmire, a BABE VOTE member, spent more than an hour on the phone with the Secretary of State’s staff troubleshooting the system as she tried to change her address on her voter registration. It took her more than a week and additional phone calls before she was able to request an absentee ballot. This is not a one-time occurrence. Many long-time voters have reported that they have been removed from the voter database, even though they have voted consistently in recent elections. So these are not hypothetical concerns. They are issues we are hearing about and experiencing ourselves. If voters are unaware of potential problems or delays, they may wait until it is too late to resolve them. BABE VOTE does not want to discourage anyone from registering or voting. Our goal is to warn legally eligible voters to start now: check your voter registration, register or re-register to vote, and make a plan to vote, whether by absentee ballot, early in person, or at the polls on Election Day. Idahoans should not have to navigate unnecessary obstacles to exercise their right to vote, but until those obstacles are addressed, voters need to know they exist. Voting should not be a last-minute scramble. Don’t wait until Election Day. Check your registration, make a plan, and give yourself time to resolve any problems so you can cast your ballot. Babe, VOTE! BABE VOTE is a non-partisan, non-profit that empowers young people to organize their communities for democracy.

Other provisions of the bill would allow student-athletes to transfer only once in their college careers; cap fees to agents at 5%; and restrict colleges and universities from cutting programs in Olympic sports in order to sink the savings into football. “College athletics are facing significant challenges Congress can and must meaningfully address,” Crapo said in a news release Tuesday. “The Protect College Sports Act provides much-needed clarity and consistency for student athletes and higher education institutions.” In the same news release, Idaho’s three university presidents took turns hailing the bill. “The Protect College Sports Act is an important pathway for creating a stable, fair foundation for college athletics,” Boise State University President David Hahn said. Despite the overwhelming Senate vote — and backing from President Donald Trump — the Protect College Sports Act is not a done deal. It still needs to pass the House, which is on recess until after the November election. If the House fails to act on the bill during a lame-duck session after the elections, ESPN noted, the process would have to start over in the next congressional session. Coming Thursday: As college athletics becomes a national political football, what’s at stake in Idaho? We take a closer look.

Read More The voter pamphlet includes information about the range of questions on the ballot — such as Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would end the state’s abortion ban and establish reproductive rights; a proposed constitutional amendment that would only allow the Legislature to legalize drugs, such as marijuana; a constitutional amendment that would declare English as the state’s official language; and an advisory question that solicits a public vote to declare a state gun. That’s along with information about key upcoming election dates, voting options and voter registration. (You can also find information about those issues, along with races for statewide constitutional offices and in select legislative districts, in the Idaho Capital Sun’s voter guide .) “Election season is underway,” Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican running for re-election, said in a statement. “Every household in Idaho can expect to receive a Voter Pamphlet with the information you need to be ready to vote in November. This special America 250 edition includes some fun nods to our history as we celebrate 250 years of America and make our mark on the future of our state. Make a plan, get registered, and vote!” To view the pamphlet online and access it in Spanish or an audio format, visit VoteIdaho.gov , a website run by the Secretary of State’s Office. It would be the first in Oregon sited on federal public land, and one of at least 12 proposed for more than 17,500 Bureau of Land Management acres across western states under President Donald Trump’s July 2025 executive order to hasten data center development. The proposals on federal land in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming were first reported last week by The Washington Sun, whose reporters reviewed difficult to find right-of-way requests via BLM’s Mineral and Land Records System . The bulk of federally managed land in the U.S. is in the West, including in Oregon where half the state’s land is owned and managed by the federal government. Oregon is among the top 10 markets for data centers in the U.S., according to Pew Research. Under the executive order, Trump mandated that federally owned land and resources be used for “the expeditious and orderly development of data centers (…) to be used in service of the prosperity and security of the American people.” It’s the first time the Bureau of Land Management, tasked with managing more than 245 million public acres for uses that include animal grazing, timber harvesting and recreation, has been ordered to include data centers in its portfolio. Several months after Trump issued the order, the California-based energy company Copia, which has an office in Lake Oswego, submitted an application to site the Charlestown Data Center and Battery Energy Storage System in Umatilla County on 106 acres of BLM land. The company most recently submitted a draft plan for development of the data center project on May 8, 2026, available only via federal public records request, according to Sarah Bennett, a spokesperson for the bureau’s Northwest region office. items.body: An independent conservative running in a swing district against a Republican incumbent and a Democratic challenger means anything could happen in November. Rep. Mike Pohanka, R-Jerome, narrowly won the 2024 general election over Democrat Ned Burns by 2.4 percentage points. Pohanka now faces a three-way race against a Democrat with a long career in education and a Christian conservative independent who believes the government has turned away from God. Pohanka is seeking a second term in District 26 House Seat A. District 26 includes blue voters in Blaine County and red voters to the south in Jerome and Lincoln counties. But Pohanka said he considers himself colorblind. He said he’s a public servant who wants to help his constituents. “I have people coming up to me saying, ‘You know what? I’m a Democrat, and I’m voting for you because you are a person that cares and you’re doing the job,'” Pohanka said. That attitude encouraged independent Bella Schiffler to run. She interned for two lawmakers in Boise and said she learned that many politicians who call themselves conservative aren’t really conservative. Schiffler said education has become “woke,” citing a debunked hoax about litter boxes in schools. She told EdNews that she would be in favor of taking away women’s right to vote if it helped the country move closer to God. “America is a Christian nation, and we are founded on godly principles,” Schiffler said. Pohanka said he hopes Schiffler will not split the conservative vote in November, which happened two years ago when her aunt, Kala Tate, ran for the Senate as an independent. Anita Janis, chair of the Jerome County Democrats, wants to bring her experiences of teaching around the country to the Legislature. She said Idaho can learn from other states, where education funding works differently. “I have lived in other states where there would never be a levy put together to support salaries,” Janis said. She wants to see the Legislature fulfill its duty under the Idaho Constitution to fund public schools. Election Day is Nov. 3. But on Friday, lawmakers slammed the brakes on those applications and the $1.2 million program. The Rural Health Transformation Committee put the behavioral health hubs on hold — at least until the 2027 legislative session, which begins in January. Committee members said the hub proposal represents a policy change and lawmakers should have the chance to vote on it. The $1.2 million is a small part of Idaho’s $186 million rural health bank account — Phase One of a five-year, federally funded grant program . But Friday’s committee discussion underscores a bigger debate over the funds. The Department of Health and Welfare is racing to commit the $186 million by the feds’ Oct. 30 deadline. (Photo courtesy of Sarah Wood/U.S. Department of Energy) Editor’s Note: This is the first installment of a three-part Idaho Capital Sun series examining the proposal to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Part one focuses on Gov. Brad Little’s role in negotiations and his priorities for Idaho. The series continues Monday and Tuesday with a closer look at the cases for and against bringing a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Idaho Gov. Brad Little said he will not jeopardize the health of the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer or the health of Idahoans as he continues to negotiate potentially bringing a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. “I’ve had this direct conversation with Secretary (of Energy Chris) Wright: Disposal of spent fuel over the aquifer in Idaho – that’s a nonstarter,” Little said in an interview Wednesday at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. In July, U.S. Department of Energy officials announced that Idaho is one of five states selected as a finalist to host one of the new innovation campuses. Little signed a memorandum of understanding in July with the U.S. Department of Energy, or DOE, to hold formal discussions and negotiations about bringing an innovation campus to Idaho. The Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer is outlined in orange of this map of Washington, Oregon and Idaho. (Map courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey) If Idaho is selected as a host site, the federal government has said the state will have to accept shipments of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste from other states. A Request for Information Response that Little signed and submitted to the federal government in March describes an accelerated process that takes “months rather than decades” to bring the “initial capabilities” of a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus online in 2027. But on Wednesday, Little said things aren’t moving that quickly. “There’s a long way to go before this happens,” Little said. “(The DOE) would love to identify some sites, and I believe … they may need something by the end of the year. But it will not be in any way, shape or form a final agreement.” Little said the documents he signed do not obligate Idaho to host an innovation campus or accept nuclear fuel or radioactive waste. Instead, the agreements simply bring Idaho to the negotiating table, the governor said. Little said it makes sense for Idaho to be at the negotiating table because of the potential economic benefits to the state, the infrastructure, the experience at Idaho National Laboratory in eastern Idaho and the need for additional, reliable energy. The memorandum of understanding lists a Sept. 30 deadline, but Little said he doesn’t think agreements will be reached that quickly, and he suggested the two sides could either continue talks or sign another memorandum of understanding with a later deadline. Officials at Idaho National Laboratory declined to comment for this series of articles. What is a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus? items.body: The Boise School District says it could close a number of schools, convert others, and revamp which grades attend high school and junior high as it faces declining enrollment. The district rolled out a number of proposals during virtual and in-person meetings this week it called “The Future of Boise Schools.” Meeting invitations didn’t hint at the scale of the proposed changes, but did note that final decisions have not been made. The proposals include shutting down or combining some grade schools, closing several junior high schools, moving high schools from three years to four, and possibly adding a specialized new high school. Declining enrollment Tracy Richter, a consultant, works with school districts across the country, which all face the same issue. “We don’t have a district that we’re working with anywhere in the country that is rising in enrollment,” Richter said, which he attributed to a decline in birth rates across the country. Factors like housing availability are also affecting school district enrollment — families may be holding onto homes longer, even after children have grown up and moved out, and young families may struggle to afford the homes that are available. When costs are prohibitive for young families to move in, it does not lead to more students for the district, Richter said. The housing market, Richter said, creates another barrier for families looking to move. “Nobody wants to go to half the house for twice the money and four times the interest rate.” Richter works for HPM, a consulting company contracted by the Boise School District to create a Long-Range Facilities Master Plan. The Boise School District currently has 9,000 open seats, 5,000 of which are at the elementary school level. Part of the plan aims to propose solutions to declining student enrollment, which is creating excess capacity, particularly at the district’s elementary and junior high schools. To do so, HPM has developed and is seeking public feedback on three potential scenarios: addressing excess capacity at the high school level, junior high level, or elementary school level. The company also developed “concepts,” or ways to implement each scenario, including closing some elementary schools in the district, moving 9th grade from the junior high to high school level, and changing enrollment areas and boundaries for schools. Richter presented each of the scenarios at a virtual and in-person meetings this week. District patrons are being encouraged to review the potential scenarios and concepts and submit their feedback via a Fall Community Survey , available on the district’s master planning webpage . Richter said that his team received 900 responses from an initial survey in the spring, which helped them develop the scenarios under consideration now. Richter anticipated it would take until February or March to develop a facilities master plan and make a recommendation that the district’s board of trustees would then adopt. “What we want people to understand is that we’re not even close to any recommendations yet,” Richter said, “and we want to make sure that we are doing as transparent of a process as we can to make sure we’re getting as much input as we can from the community.” The district could make decisions on any potential funding needed to implement the changes, such as bonds, after the master plan is established, Richter said. He estimated it could take two to five years for the district to implement any recommendation.
